title: Percentage, Profit & Loss
intro: Percentage is the language of SSC arithmetic — profit and loss, discount, data interpretation and even ratio all speak it. Treat a percentage as a fraction (25% = 1/4, 12.5% = 1/8) and most sums collapse to one line. Profit and loss then layer on three prices — cost, marked and selling — with the single golden rule that profit and loss percent are ALWAYS taken on the cost price. Master the multiplier idea (a 20% rise means x 1.2) and you will out-pace the calculator.

topics.name: Percentage Basics & Conversions
topics.details: Percent means per hundred. Convert between percent, fraction and decimal fluently: 50% = 1/2 = 0.5, 33.33% = 1/3, 12.5% = 1/8, 16.66% = 1/6, 6.25% = 1/16. Memorising these fraction equivalents turns 'find 37.5% of 240' into '3/8 of 240 = 90' instantly. To find what percent A is of B, compute A/B x 100.

solved.problem: If 15% of a number is 45, find the number.

unsolved.problem: 40% of a number is 64. The number?

topics.name: Percentage Change
topics.details: A percentage increase then a decrease (or vice versa) does NOT cancel out. If a value rises by a% and then falls by a%, the net change is a loss of (a^2/100)%. Successive changes multiply factors: a 20% rise and a 10% rise give x 1.2 x 1.1 = x 1.32, a net 32% rise. For population/price problems, chain the multipliers.

solved.problem: A salary is increased by 20% then decreased by 20%. Net change?
A price rises 10% then rises another 20%. Overall rise?
If length increases 25% and breadth decreases 20%, change in area?
A number is increased by 50% and the result decreased by 40%. Net?

unsolved.problem: Side of a square increased 20%. Area change?

topics.name: Profit, Loss & Cost Price
topics.details: Profit = SP - CP, Loss = CP - SP, and crucially profit% and loss% are taken on the COST price. To get SP from a profit%, multiply CP by (1 + p/100). To recover CP from SP and a profit%, divide SP by (1 + p/100). When equal numbers of articles are bought and sold at different rates, set up per-unit cost and selling values.

solved.problem: Buy at 5 each, want 40% profit. SP each?
An article is sold for 1020 at a 15% loss. Find CP.
By selling at 270 a man gains 8%. Find CP.

topics.name: Discount & Marked Price
topics.details: Marked price (MP, the listed price) minus discount gives the selling price. Discount% is on MP, not on CP. A single discount of d% multiplies MP by (1 - d/100). Two successive discounts multiply: SP = MP(1 - d1/100)(1 - d2/100); they are equivalent to a single discount of d1 + d2 - (d1 d2)/100. A common SSC layer is mark-up then discount: SP = CP(1 + markup%)(1 - discount%).

solved.problem: A shopkeeper marks 40% above cost and gives 10% discount. Profit %?
Single discount equal to two successive discounts of 20% and 25%?

shortcuts: a% up then a% down = net (a^2/100)% loss.
Profit% and loss% are on COST; discount% is on MARKED price.
Mark-up then discount: SP = CP x (1 + m%) x (1 - d%).
Two discounts d1, d2 -> single = d1 + d2 - d1 d2 / 100.
mistakes: Taking profit% on the selling price instead of the cost price.
Adding two successive discounts (20% + 25% is NOT 45%).
Forgetting an a%-up then a%-down leaves a net loss, not zero.
Confusing marked price with cost price in mark-up sums.
pyq: SSC mixes percentage with profit-loss and DI every cycle. A classic Tier-2 pattern: mark goods x% above cost, give a discount, and still earn a stated profit — set up CP = 100 and solve for the unknown.
summary: Convert percentages to fractions, chain changes by multiplying factors, and remember profit/loss are on cost while discount is on marked price. Mark-up-then-discount problems reduce to CP x (1 + m%) x (1 - d%). These rules cover the highest-frequency SSC arithmetic block.
